questions.q: Why does this lesson say a pure checklist mindset ("is the control present, yes or no") fails at the architecture level?
options: A checklist always overstates how secure a system actually is
It has no way to represent that every control carries real costs, and that the right amount of security differs by business and by system
Checklists are too difficult for most engineers to complete accurately
Checklists are only used by auditors and have no relevance to technical teams
questions.explain: A checklist treats every control as free and universally desirable, with no mechanism for weighing cost against risk reduction for a specific business and system.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the three real costs every security control carries?
options: Legal liability, headcount turnover, and brand reputation
Vendor lock-in, data residency, and audit frequency
Downtime, documentation burden, and training time
Friction (usability tax), money (licensing/infrastructure/headcount), and complexity (a new moving part that can itself fail or become a target)
questions.explain: The lesson identifies friction, money, and complexity as the three real, ongoing costs behind every control, not just the one-time cost of implementing it.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call complexity the cost architects most often underweight?
options: Because complexity only matters for very small organizations, not enterprises
Because adding more controls can never introduce new risk
Because a new control, like a secrets vault, is itself a new moving part that needs its own availability plan, access controls, and patching — a new source of risk
Because complexity costs are always lower than friction costs in practice
questions.explain: Every added control is a new system that can fail, misconfigure, drift, or become a target itself — a genuine security improvement can still introduce a new source of operational and security risk.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the single biggest real-world cause of security controls quietly failing?
options: Legitimate users routing around unbearable friction into shadow IT, which is often less secure and invisible to monitoring
Insufficient logging retention periods
A lack of sufficiently advanced attacker tooling
Controls being too cheap to implement properly
questions.explain: The lesson argues that ignoring friction cost doesn't produce more security — it pushes legitimate users toward unsanctioned workarounds that are frequently less secure and outside the visibility of existing controls.

questions.q: What is a documented risk acceptance, as described in this lesson?
options: A technical workaround that eliminates the need for a control entirely
A ticket closed by the engineer who implemented the related control
A quarterly report sent only to the security team with no business sign-off
A record of the gap being left open, the reason, the residual risk, and a named accountable business owner signing off on carrying that risk, instead of silently skipping the control
questions.explain: A risk acceptance is the honest, defensible alternative to quietly skipping a control: it documents the gap, the reasoning, and gets sign-off from an accountable business owner rather than the architect alone.
